newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seen placing more debt, paying more to IMF.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seen placing more debt, paying more to IMF.

text.p: Mexico's fast-paced placement of bonds so far this year is part of a "tidal wave" of investor money that has washed up on the shores of Latin America, economists said on Monday.
They said Mexico will continue to take advantage of the hot market conditions to raise cash and will likely speed up its payment schedule to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The federal government could place about another $3.0 billion of additional debt in international capital markets this year, using most of the proceeds to make more prepayments to the IMF, Santander Investment said in a report.
"Mexico will be placing more debt... most likely to repay more to the IMF," Santander Investment economist Hector Chavez told Reuters on Monday .

The federal government only has about $1.4 billion in maturing debt coming due in 1997 -- a yen bond in March, a U.S. dollar floating rate note in July, and another tranche of a yen issue in December.
"Their needs are not very great, but the numbers could be higher if they decide to go ahead with more prepayments to the IMF," ING Barings' Americas chief economist Arturo Porzecanski told Reuters.
ING Barings released figures on Monday showing that to Feb. 21, Latin American international bond issuance -- Eurobonds, Yankees and Globals -- totalled $12.03 billion so far this year.
New bonds issued by sovereigns accounted for two-thirds of that amount.

ING Barings called the amount astounding and far and away an all-time record for a short eight-week period. This follows on the heels of a record $51.4 billion placed by Latin American borrowers last year.
Argentina holds the record as the busiest Latin American borrower, but Mexico runs a close second.
In January the federal government, the United Mexican States (UMS), placed a 10-year global issue worth $1.0 billion, and a 10-year Italian lira bond worth about $300 million.
Then this month the UMS has placed a 12-year mark bond issue worth about $880 million, and a seven-year yen-denominated bond issue in the Samurai market worth about $400 million.

The government has found no shortage of uses for its cash from debt placements late last year and this, such as paying down the $3.5 billion it owed to the U.S. Treasury, and $1.5 billion to the IMF in January.

Last week it announced it would pay another $590 million to the IMF, with the $1.18 billion it received from the most recent lira and mark issues, placing the remainder in the nation's international reserves "to meet future debt maturities."
Before the announcement of the most recent $590 million payback to the IMF, Mexico said in January it owed $11.609 billion to that organization. Of that only $827 million was coming due in 1997.
As well as meeting maturing debt, Mexico also bought back some outstanding Brady bonds last year.
However, last week Mexico's deputy finance minister Martin Werner told analysts that the government was not considering another buyback of the Brady bonds in the short-term.
Other Mexican borrowers, such as state-owned oil company Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex), and government development banks, Bancomext and Nafin, are also seen going to the markets this year.
With Mexico showing a strong economic rebound, analysts say they see these borrowers, and the UMS, having no problem continuing to place as much paper as needed.
